html:
This verse — Rabbi-rḥamhumā kamā rabbayānī ṣaghīran ("My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small") — is not from the Prophetic sunna in the way most duas on this site are. It is Qur'an 17:24, the final clause of a two-ayah passage (Al-Isrāʾ 17:23–24) in which Allah teaches believers how to speak and act toward their parents. The dua is Allah's own words placed on the believer's tongue, which is why al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr both class it as the highest and most binding kind of prayer: a dua whose text, grammar, and shape were chosen by the One being addressed.

The passage opens with a universal command: wa-qaḍā rabbuka allā taʿbudū illā iyyāhu wa-bi-l-wālidayni iḥsānan — "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, kindness." Classical mufassirūn draw attention to the grammatical juxtaposition. The command to tawḥīd (allā taʿbudū illā iyyāhu) and the command to parental kindness (wa-bi-l-wālidayni iḥsānan) are joined by a simple wāw, without a dividing clause. Ibn Kathīr (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, on 17:23) comments that this placement is deliberate: honoring parents is Allah's chosen illustration of what tawḥīd looks like in practice. A heart that has truly submitted to its Creator will submit to the mercy its Creator placed in the womb and the household that raised it. The verse does not say "AND tawḥīd AND kindness to parents"; it says "worship Him — AND [as part of that worship, as its first social fruit] be good to your parents."

The ayah then narrows to a specific scenario — the one most likely to test the believer: immā yablughanna ʿindaka l-kibara aḥaduhumā aw kilāhumā fa-lā taqul lahumā uffin wa-lā tanharhumā wa-qul lahumā qawlan karīman. "If one of them, or both, reach old age with you, do not say to them uff, nor rebuke them, but speak to them a noble word." Al-Qurṭubī (al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, on 17:23) records a point that is often missed: Allah did not say when they reach old age — He said ʿindaka, "with you." The construction obligates the adult child to keep the parent in proximity. A culture that outsources elderly care to institutions can satisfy the literal command "do not say uff" by placing distance between parent and child so that no uff is ever uttered. The Qur'anic preposition closes that loophole. Old-age kindness is to happen in the son's or daughter's home, within earshot, within reach of a hand.

The word uff is itself a small lesson. The classical lexicographers (al-Zamakhsharī in al-Kashshāf, Ibn Manẓūr in Lisān al-ʿArab) note it is not a curse, not a shout, not a blow — it is the smallest audible sound of annoyance in the Arabic language, roughly a tsk or a sigh of impatience. The jurists derive from this a minore-ad-maius principle (bāb al-tanbīh bi-l-adnā ʿalā l-aʿlā): if the Qur'an forbids the smallest audible annoyance toward an aging parent, then everything louder — a raised voice, a sarcastic remark, a slammed door, a dismissive gesture — is a fortiori forbidden. Al-Qurṭubī writes that this is the only verse in the Qur'an where Allah forbids a sound this small, and the only one where He pairs the prohibition with a positive command to speak qawlan karīman — "a noble word." The scholarly consensus is that karīm here means language chosen for the parent's dignity, not merely for truthfulness. You may be factually correct and still speak unlawfully if the correctness is delivered in a way that strips honor.

Then comes verse 24, which contains the dua on this page: wa-khfiḍ lahumā janāḥa-dh-dhulli min ar-raḥmah wa-qul rabbi-rḥamhumā kamā rabbayānī ṣaghīran. "And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me small." The image khafḍ janāḥ al-dhull ("lowering the wing of humility") is a Qur'anic metaphor also used of Prophets toward believers (wa-khfiḍ janāḥaka li-man ittabaʿaka min al-muʾminīn, Al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:215). Ibn Kathīr explains: a bird lowers its wing to shelter its young; the believer is commanded to lower his wing to shelter his parents. The role-reversal is explicit. The one who was sheltered becomes the shelter. This is not merely sentimental — the verse specifies min ar-raḥmah, "out of mercy." The humility must be motivated by compassion for them, not performed as a social duty, not calculated as inheritance strategy, not displayed for the extended family's approval.

The dua itself — rabbi-rḥamhumā kamā rabbayānī ṣaghīran — carries a precise grammatical weight. The verb rabbayānī ("they raised me") shares a root (r-b-w) with one of Allah's most repeated names, al-Rabb. The semantic field of r-b-w covers nurturing, raising, feeding, educating, and bringing to maturity. By choosing this verb, the Qur'an is drawing a parallel: parents performed, in their small and limited sphere, the kind of work Allah performs cosmically — the raising of a dependent creature into a mature one. The dua asks Allah to extend His mercy toward them kamā — "in the same way as" — they extended their raising-work toward the child. Al-Rāzī (Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb, on 17:24) comments that the kāf here is not literal equivalence — no human raising can be the equal of divine mercy — but a petition that Allah's mercy be aligned with and inclusive of the specific trouble parents took in raising this specific child. The childhood is not generic; it is ṣaghīran, "small-sized" — the small child, the small cries, the small needs, the specific small life that two people spent decades building.

Who is the dua for? The grammatical form lahumā ("for the two of them") in verse 23, and rabbayānī ("they-two raised me") in verse 24, use the Arabic dual (muthannā), referring explicitly to both parents. Al-Qurṭubī records a question raised by early jurists: can this dua be prayed if one or both parents are non-Muslim, deceased, or no longer in contact with the child? The majority position (al-Qurṭubī, al-Nawawī in al-Majmūʿ, Ibn Taymiyyah in Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā) distinguishes between duʿāʾ al-raḥmah fī al-dunyā (asking Allah to extend worldly mercy — guidance, health, provision, forgiveness-if-they-repent) and duʿāʾ al-maghfirah ākhira (asking for after-death forgiveness). The first is permissible for any parent, living or deceased, Muslim or not. The second — explicit forgiveness-dua after death — is permissible only for Muslim parents, following the clear boundary set in Qur'an 9:113. For deceased Muslim parents, this dua becomes among the most consequential acts of ongoing charity (ṣadaqah jāriyah) that a child can perform, as recorded in the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah: idhā māta l-insānu nqaṭaʿa ʿanhu ʿamaluhu illā min thalāthatin: ṣadaqah jāriyah, aw ʿilmun yuntafaʿu bihi, aw waladun ṣāliḥun yadʿū lahu ("When a person dies, his deeds come to an end except from three: continuing charity, knowledge benefitted from, or a righteous child who prays for him" — Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1631).

The Prophet ﷺ singled out parental piety (birr al-wālidayn) as among the most beloved deeds to Allah. Ibn Masʿūd narrates: "I asked the Prophet ﷺ which deed is most beloved to Allah. He said: al-ṣalātu ʿalā waqtihā (prayer at its time). I said: then what? He said: birru l-wālidayn (kindness to parents). I said: then what? He said: al-jihādu fī sabīlillāh (struggle in Allah's path)" (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 527 and Muslim 85). The Prophet ﷺ placed birr al-wālidayn above jihad — above, that is, the paradigmatic deed of self-sacrifice — because the lifelong, mundane, unglamorous work of being kind to an aging parent is itself a form of struggle whose reward Allah tracks with unusual care. Another ḥadīth, from Abū Hurayrah (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2551), is even sharper: the Prophet ﷺ said three times "raghima anfu" ("may his nose be rubbed in dust" — a Prophetic idiom for severe loss) and when asked whose nose, he replied: man adraka abawayhi ʿinda l-kibari aḥadahumā aw kilayhimā thumma lam yadkhul al-jannah — "whoever reaches [the condition of having] one or both parents in old age and then does not enter paradise." The ḥadīth makes aging parents a cause of paradise — a door placed in your path, which is why losing the opportunity through neglect is treated as a catastrophic failure.

When to pray this dua? The sunna attached is less formally structured than, say, the morning adhkār or the before-sleep formula, but classical practice is clear on three contexts. First, after the five obligatory prayers — Ibn al-Qayyim in Zād al-Maʿād notes that the post-prayer adhkār period is a time of accepted supplication, and prayer for parents during this window was the regular practice of the salaf. Second, during the night prayer (tahajjud) and in sujūd — the Prophet ﷺ taught that the servant is closest to his Lord while prostrating (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 482), and extended family-dua in this position is well-attested in biographical reports of the companions. Third, on specific days of divine proximity: Fridays (especially the last hour before Maghrib), the day of ʿArafah, and the final third of every night. For deceased parents, the dua becomes an act of ongoing worship — recited at graves (where the ḥadīth of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 974 encourages the standard greeting-dua for the dead), and incorporated into the regular ongoing supplication of the living child. Al-Nawawī in al-Adhkār records that it was the practice of the salaf to never let a full day pass without a dua for parents, living or deceased.

A pastoral note that classical scholars raise honestly: Qur'an 17:24 does not promise reconciliation, cure, or an easy relationship. The scenario the preceding ayah paints — ʿindaka l-kibar, an aging parent in your home — is often emotionally hard. Scholars from Ibn al-Jawzī (Birr al-Wālidayn) to contemporary fiqh councils acknowledge that parents, like all humans, can be unjust, difficult, verbally harsh, or in extreme cases abusive. The Qur'anic command is iḥsān (goodness) and qawlan karīman (noble speech), not blind compliance. The limiting principle comes two surahs later: wa-in jāhadāka ʿalā an tushrika bī mā laysa laka bihī ʿilmun fa-lā tuṭiʿhumā wa-ṣāḥibhumā fī d-dunyā maʿrūfan — "if they strive to make you associate with Me what you have no knowledge of, do not obey them, but accompany them in this world with kindness" (Qur'an 31:15). Obedience is suspended where sin is commanded; kindness is not. The dua rabbi-rḥamhumā remains binding even when the relationship is painful, even where boundaries must be enforced — because the dua asks Allah to extend His mercy to them, not asks you to extend your presence without limit.

Does the dua "work" in the measurable sense a Western reader might ask about? Does praying rabbi-rḥamhumā lengthen a parent's life, soften their temperament, cure their illness? The classical answer is honest: Allah hears the dua and responds in one of three ways, as the Prophet ﷺ said in the ḥadīth narrated by Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: "There is no Muslim who makes a dua that does not contain sin or breaking of family ties, except that Allah grants him one of three: either He gives him what he asked for in this world, or He stores it for him in the hereafter, or He turns away from him an equivalent evil" (Musnad Aḥmad 11133, authenticated as ḥasan by al-Albānī and Shuʿayb al-Arnāʾūṭ). The dua does not guarantee a specific worldly outcome. What it guarantees is that something happens: a worldly answer, a stored eternal reward, or a hidden protection. For deceased parents, the dua enters a different economy — it reaches them as ṣadaqah, it adds to their book of deeds in a way that does not depend on them having done anything in response. The child's prayer continues to raise them.

What this dua is not: it is not a magical formula that erases the hard work of showing up. The Qur'an is explicit that the words come after the wing of humility (wa-khfiḍ lahumā janāḥa-dh-dhulli min ar-raḥmah wa-qul rabbi-rḥamhumā — the wa-qul ("and say") is sequenced after the khafḍ al-janāḥ). The dua is the crown on an action, not a substitute for it. A believer who prays rabbi-rḥamhumā but will not visit, will not call, will not spend, will not endure a difficult conversation has, in the view of al-Qurṭubī and al-Nawawī, prayed a dua whose preconditions he has not met. Conversely, a believer who does the hard work of birr al-wālidayn and makes this dua regularly has engaged in one of the highest spiritual exchanges the Qur'an offers — small-scale raising, aligned with Allah's cosmic raising, requested back as mercy.
